title: How do you decide whether a client should make a big investment?
description: "Should the client make this investment?" A new plant, more capacity, a system, a store or a piece of equipment.
hook: Investment cases ask whether something is worth the money: a new factory, a new route, a big IT system. They come down to whether the benefits outweigh the cost, and how sure we can be. Here is how to structure one.
body:
When you will use it

A new plant, more capacity, a system, a store or a piece of equipment.

This is a decide question: "Should we do this?" Test it against a few yes/no questions, put a number on it, and end with a clear yes or no. More on the three families of case questions.

Ask this first

What does it cost upfront, and what does it change: revenue, costs, or both?

The structure

  • Do we need it?
    • Is demand real and lasting?
    • Can we get more from what we have? (fix bottlenecks · extra shifts)
  • Will it pay? (if rivals add capacity too, prices may fall)
    • Upfront and running costs
    • Extra revenue or savings
  • Is there a better alternative?
    • Outsource or subcontract
    • Lease or rent
  • Can we deliver it?
    • Time to build
    • Skills and risks

Make it your own

Payback = upfront cost ÷ yearly net gain. Break-even volume = upfront cost ÷ extra margin per unit. Compare both with the client's target and the asset's life.

The mistake to avoid

Approving new capacity before checking whether existing capacity can be squeezed.

Practise with real prompts

1. Should a car maker build its own battery plant?

Show a model structure
  • Need: Our battery demand and supply security; Prices and lead times from suppliers
  • Make vs buy economics: Plant cost vs buying, per kWh; Payback and NPV
  • Risks: Technology changing fast; Can we run a plant at scale?
  • Alternatives: Joint venture, long-term supply contracts; Buying a stake in a supplier

Where to start: Make vs buy cost per kWh over the life of the plant.

The trap: Ignoring that battery technology may change before the plant pays back.

2. Should an airline launch a co-branded credit card?

Show a model structure
  • Customer value: Who would use it; Points earned and redeemed
  • Economics: Bank pays us per card and per point; Cost of rewards (seats) and marketing
  • Partner: Which bank, terms, exclusivity; Risk sharing
  • Risks: Brand if the bank treats customers badly; Too many free seats given away

Where to start: Economics: what the bank pays per point vs what a reward seat costs us.

The trap: Treating it as a pure brand decision when it is mainly a points business.

3. Should a supermarket open dark stores for 15-minute delivery?

Show a model structure
  • Demand: How many orders per dark store per day; Density: orders within a 15-minute radius
  • Economics per order: Basket size, delivery fee; Picking, delivery, rent per order
  • Cannibalisation: Orders taken from our own stores and online; Net new profit
  • Competition and operations: Rapid-delivery rivals burning cash; Can we staff and stock it?

Where to start: Economics per order: rapid delivery usually loses money on every order at low volume.

The trap: Assuming every order is new and not taken from our own stores.

Compare an investment with the alternative it replaces

A manufacturer can buy equipment for £2 million to save £650,000 in labour and scrap annually. Maintenance adds £100,000 per year, so incremental annual cash benefit is £550,000 before tax. Simple payback is about 3.6 years (£2m ÷ £550k), but payback does not tell you whether the investment creates value.

At a 10% discount rate and five years of constant £550,000 cash benefits, the present value is roughly £2.1 million, giving an NPV of about £85,000 before residual value, tax and working-capital effects. That is a much narrower decision than the payback figure suggests.

Now stress-test the uncertain variables: does the machine actually deliver the projected efficiency? Will demand fill the available capacity? Is the equipment still useful if the product changes? Could leasing, outsourcing or process redesign achieve a comparable result for less risk? In the interview, make clear which figures are cash flows and which are accounting expenses.
